lines: In 2019, a typical home was affordable in 48 of the fifty states.
Today? 9.

The cheapest home in America isn't in the state you think, and it's not the most affordable one either.
And in 31 states, the share of income a home takes has more than doubled since 2019.
We ranked all fifty states with official numbers.
Stay to the end, and you'll see exactly where yours lands.
Lenders have an old rule of thumb.
Your housing payment shouldn't be more than twenty eight percent of what you earn before taxes.
Go above it, and a home stops being a home. It becomes a stretch.
So we tested every state against it.
The typical home listed for sale in each state over the last twelve months, from Realtor dot com.
The typical household income, from the Census Bureau.
Ten percent down, and a thirty year fixed mortgage at today's average rate, 7.24 percent, from Freddie Mac.
And we didn't even count property taxes or insurance.
The real numbers are higher than everything you're about to see.
First, the whole country.
This is the mortgage on a typical American home, as a share of a typical income, every month since 2016.
The dashed line is the twenty eight percent rule.
In January 2021, rates were under three percent, and a typical home took about eighteen percent of income.
Easy.
Then rates more than doubled. By October 2023, the same math hit thirty eight percent.
Today it's around 34.
The country as a whole is over the line. But the country is an average.
Your state isn't.

Part four. The real price tag.

There's one more way to see it. How many years of income does a typical home cost?
In Ohio, 3.3 years. In Illinois, 3.3.
In California, 7.2. In Montana, 7.3. And in New York, 7.5 years.
Every dollar a New York family earns for seven and a half years. Before taxes. Before food.
Let's make it even more concrete. A work month has about twenty two working days.

In California and Montana, about 11.5.
In Florida, 8.6. In Texas, 6.7.

In Ohio, a little over three. In Illinois, the same.

Part five. What changed.
Here's every state, then and now. Across the bottom, 2019. Up the side, today.
First, the obvious one. Every single state got worse. All fifty.
And in 31 of them, the share of income more than doubled.
In 2019, only California and Hawaii were over the line. Everyone else was fine.
Since then, Wyoming went from 16 percent to 43.
Montana, from 24 to 53. Idaho, from 22 to 49.
The states that got hit hardest weren't the expensive coasts.
Many were the cheap, quiet states people moved to when they could work from anywhere.
Prices went up there. Incomes didn't keep up. And then rates doubled.
Here are the biggest jumps in listing prices since 2019.
Wyoming, up 82 percent. Montana, 80.
New Hampshire, 77. Maine, 76. Vermont, 75.
Quiet, rural, beautiful states. Exactly the kind of place people dreamed about during the pandemic.
Meanwhile California went up 27 percent. Texas, 22. Colorado, 20.
The expensive places didn't get cheaper. The cheap places caught up.
So what would fix it? We reran every state at lower rates.
At today's rate, 9 states pass. At six percent, 17.
At five, 25. At four percent, 34.
And at three percent, where rates were in 2021, 44 states would pass again.
But even at zero percent interest, a typical New York home would still take 23 percent of income.
In some places, the rate isn't the problem. The price is.
One honest caveat.
We used listing prices, not final sale prices, and listings in places like Montana include a lot of high end homes.
The ranking at the top holds either way.
So in 2019, 48 states passed the test. Today, 9 do.
So what actually decides your number? Three things. The price of the home. Your income. And the rate.
You can't control the rate. And your income doesn't change overnight.
But the price depends almost entirely on where you buy.
The same household income that fails in New York passes easily in Ohio. Same family, 55 percent versus 24.
And if rates ever fall back to six percent, the number of passing states almost doubles, from 9 to 17.
The top three hardest states today: New York, Montana and California.
The three easiest: Ohio, Illinois, and Iowa and Nebraska tied for third.
And the last state standing?
Ohio. Where a typical home still costs less than a quarter of a paycheck.
